Monte Carlo Integration: Session Exercises

Module 1, Day 1 — DATASCI 406, Computational Methods in Statistics and Data Science

Mark M. Fredrickson (mfredric@umich.edu)

Exercise 1 builds your toolbox of samplers. Every exercise after it uses the recipe from the video:

  1. Write the integral as \(\text{E}\left(h(X)\right)\) for a random variable \(X\) you can sample.
  2. Sample \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) and average \(h(X_i)\).
  3. Report a confidence interval, not just the point estimate.

Each integration exercise has a known true value, so you can check your work. Your estimates will differ from the targets — that is the point. Your confidence interval should usually cover the target.

1. A tour of R’s distributions

Let’s investigate the distributions available in R. ?Distributions lists every distribution R ships with; each has the r/d/p/q functions from the video.

Exercise

(a) Here is a start on a catalog of draws, in the long format that ggplot likes:

n <- 1000
draws <- list(
  norm   = rnorm(n),
  unif   = runif(n),
  exp    = rexp(n),
  cauchy = rcauchy(n)
) |> enframe() |> unnest(value)

draws |> group_by(name) |> summarize(mean(value))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   name   `mean(value)`
#>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 cauchy      -5.75   
#> 2 exp          1.02   
#> 3 norm         0.00762
#> 4 unif         0.504

Extend the list with at least six more distributions from the ?Distributions page, mixing continuous and discrete. Most need parameters — check the help page (e.g. ?rgamma) and pick any sensible values; skip rmultinom (it returns a matrix). Then plot the whole catalog as histograms in one faceted figure (facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free")).

The Cauchy panel will look broken — one bar and a huge empty axis. It is not a bug. Investigate:

  • Re-run your summarize() of the sample means a few times. Every other distribution’s mean barely moves between runs. What does the Cauchy’s do?
  • Look at sort(abs(rcauchy(n)), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5] a few times. Where is the histogram’s x-axis coming from?

(b) Pick two distributions from your catalog and explore their parameters, plotting draws across a grid of parameter values. Here is the pattern, applied to the Normal — expand_grid() builds every combination, and map2() draws a sample for each row:

expand_grid(mean = c(-5, 0, 5), sd = c(0.5, 2)) |>
  mutate(value = map2(mean, sd, ~ rnorm(2000, mean = .x, sd = .y))) |>
  unnest(value) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_grid(sd ~ mean, labeller = label_both)

Adapt it to two distributions of your choice (not the Normal). For at least one of them, find parameter settings that make it match a distribution you already know.

Solution

Six additions (any mix works; ?Distributions has more):

draws <- bind_rows(
  draws,
  list(
    beta    = rbeta(n, 2, 2),
    binom   = rbinom(n, 10, 0.3),
    chisq   = rchisq(n, 3),
    gamma   = rgamma(n, 2),
    pois    = rpois(n, 4),
    weibull = rweibull(n, 2)
  ) |> enframe() |> unnest(value)
)

draws |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free")

The Cauchy investigation:

replicate(5, mean(rcauchy(n)))
#> [1] 2485.0408664    0.5514392   -1.1212609   -5.8830904    0.3343285
sort(abs(rcauchy(n)), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
#> [1] 1176.7599  921.4348  664.1097  497.4999  226.1054

Every run of n = 1000 draws contains a few values hundreds of units from zero, and the histogram’s axis stretches to hold them, crushing the bulk of the data into one bar. The sample mean never settles down, no matter how often you re-run it — the Cauchy’s tails are so heavy that \(\text{E}\left(|X|\right) = \infty\): it has no mean, so there is nothing for the sample mean to converge to. The law of large numbers needs \(\text{E}\left(X\right)\) to exist, and here it does not. The Cauchy returns in exercise 6 as the way Monte Carlo breaks.

For the parameter exploration, the Beta is the one to know for this module — its two parameters bend it into most shapes a distribution on \([0, 1]\) can take:

expand_grid(alpha = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5), beta = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5)) |>
  mutate(value = map2(alpha, beta, ~ rbeta(2000, .x, .y))) |>
  unnest(value) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_grid(alpha ~ beta, labeller = label_both)

\(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\) is exactly \(U(0, 1)\) — the uniform is a special case. The project’s Part B relies on this family, so keep the picture in mind.

And the Gamma, whose shape parameter moves it from spiked to bell-shaped:

expand_grid(shape = c(0.5, 1, 2, 10)) |>
  mutate(value = map(shape, ~ rgamma(2000, .x))) |>
  unnest(value) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_wrap(~ shape, nrow = 1, scales = "free", labeller = label_both)

\(\text{Gamma}(1)\) is \(\text{Exp}(1)\) — another special case, the same way the uniform sits inside the Beta family.

2. An integral on [0, 1]

For an integral over \([0,1]\), \(\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx = \text{E}\left(g(U)\right)\), where \(U\) is uniform on \([0, 1]\). We can estimate the value of this integral by taking a sample of IID uniform draws and computing the sample mean of \(g(U_i)\).

Exercise

Estimate \[\theta = \int_0^1 \sin(\pi x) \, dx\] using 10,000 uniform draws. Give a 95% confidence interval using t.test.

The true value is \(2/\pi \approx 0.6366\). Does your interval cover it?

Solution

us <- runif(10000)
gs <- sin(pi * us)
mean(gs)
#> [1] 0.6386709
t.test(gs)$conf.int
#> [1] 0.6326290 0.6447127
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
2 / pi
#> [1] 0.6366198

The interval covers \(2/\pi\). It should, about 95% of the time.

3. Same integral, two RVs

The general recipe works with any density \(f\) that is positive on the domain: \(\int g(x)\,dx = \text{E}\left(g(X)/f(X)\right)\) for \(X \sim f\). Different choices of \(f\) give different estimators of the same integral. Are they equally good?

Exercise

Estimate \[\theta = \int_0^\infty x^2 e^{-x} \, dx\] (true value \(\Gamma(3) = 2! = 2\)) twice, with 10,000 draws each:

(a) with $f = $ Exp(1) draws (rexp / dexp), and

(b) with $f = $ Gamma(shape 2, rate 1) draws (rgamma / dgamma) — the Gamma family from exercise 1.

Before coding, simplify \(h(x) = g(x)/f(x)\) by hand in each case — both simplify pleasantly.

(c) Report a 95% confidence interval for each. Both estimate the same \(\theta\) from the same number of draws — which interval is narrower, and by roughly what factor?

(d) Plot the ECDFs of the 10,000 \(h\) values from (a) and the 10,000 from (b) on one set of axes (stat_ecdf()). What do the two curves have in common, and how does their difference explain (c)?

(e) Repeat with $f = $ Gamma(shape 3, rate 1). Something strange happens — run it, then explain.

Solution

g <- function(x) { x^2 * exp(-x) }
xs1 <- rexp(10000)
h1 <- g(xs1) / dexp(xs1)          # simplifies to xs1^2
xs2 <- rgamma(10000, shape = 2)
h2 <- g(xs2) / dgamma(xs2, 2)     # simplifies to xs2
mean(h1)
#> [1] 2.014944
mean(h2)
#> [1] 1.979856
t.test(h1)$conf.int
#> [1] 1.928604 2.101284
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
t.test(h2)$conf.int
#> [1] 1.952471 2.007240
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95

By hand: \(h_1(x) = x^2 e^{-x}/e^{-x} = x^2\), and since the Gamma(2) density is \(x e^{-x}\), \(h_2(x) = x^2 e^{-x} / (x e^{-x}) = x\). The Gamma(2) interval is about 3 times narrower from the same 10,000 draws: \(\text{Var}\left(X^2\right) = 20\) under Exp(1) versus \(\text{Var}\left(X\right) = 2\) under Gamma(2), and CI width scales with the standard deviation, \(\sqrt{20/2} \approx 3.2\).

tibble(h = c(h1, h2),
       envelope = rep(c("Exp(1)", "Gamma(2)"), each = 10000)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = h, color = envelope)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 15))

Both ECDFs are centered on the same place — both estimators are unbiased for \(\theta = 2\) — but the Exp(1) curve rises slowly with a long tail to the right, while the Gamma(2) curve climbs steeply. Same target, less spread per draw, narrower interval. Two estimators of the same quantity can differ a lot in how much each sample is worth — the next video calls this efficiency, and spends all its time engineering it.

(e) The Gamma(3) density is \(x^2 e^{-x} / 2\) — proportional to the integrand itself. So \[h_3(x) = \frac{x^2 e^{-x}}{x^2 e^{-x} / 2} = 2 \quad \text{for every draw:}\]

xs3 <- rgamma(10000, shape = 3)
h3 <- g(xs3) / dgamma(xs3, 3)
range(h3)
#> [1] 2 2
t.test(h3)$conf.int
#> Error in `t.test.default()`:
#> ! data are essentially constant

Every draw returns exactly 2, the variance is zero, and t.test refuses to run on constant data. One draw would have given the exact answer. The perfect envelope is proportional to the integrand — but writing it down requires the normalizing constant, which is the integral we wanted. Getting close to proportional without knowing the constant is where the next video is headed.

4. Probabilities are expectations of indicators

Recall an indicator function is a function that has the value 1 if a statement is true and 0 if the statement is false. They are the mathematical equivalent of if statements and conditionals in R. An important result is that for event \(A\),

\[P(A) = E(\mathbf{1}(A))\]

In other words, we can estimate probabilities in the same way we estimate expectations.

Exercise

For \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\), estimate \[\theta = P(1 \le Z \le 2)\] using 100,000 draws.

  1. Write the indicator directly in R (no ifelse needed).
  2. Give a 99% confidence interval. Which is the right tool here, t.test or binom.test, and why?
  3. Check against the exact value from pnorm.

Solution

zs <- rnorm(100000)
hits <- (1 <= zs) & (zs <= 2)
mean(hits)
#> [1] 0.13553
binom.test(sum(hits), length(hits), conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
#> [1] 0.1327543 0.1383405
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.99
pnorm(2) - pnorm(1)
#> [1] 0.1359051

binom.test is the right tool: the indicator is a Bernoulli random variable, so the interval for a proportion applies exactly, not just through the CLT approximation.

5. Joint distributions

Nothing in the recipe is one-dimensional. A double integral is an expectation over a random pair: sample both coordinates, apply \(h\), average. When the coordinates are independent, sampling the pair is just two calls to an r function.

Exercise

(a) For \(X, Y\) independent \(U(0, 1)\), estimate the double integral \[\theta = \int_0^1 \int_0^1 |x - y| \, dx \, dy = \text{E}\left(|X - Y|\right)\] with 100,000 pairs and a 95% confidence interval. The true value is \(1/3\).

(b) For \(Z_1, Z_2\) independent \(N(0, 1)\), estimate \[P(Z_1 < Z_2 + 1)\] with a 99% confidence interval, using the right interval tool for the job. Then check it exactly: what is the distribution of \(Z_1 - Z_2\)?

Solution

xs <- runif(100000); ys <- runif(100000)
diffs <- abs(xs - ys)
mean(diffs)
#> [1] 0.3323452
t.test(diffs)$conf.int
#> [1] 0.3308854 0.3338050
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
z1 <- rnorm(100000); z2 <- rnorm(100000)
hits <- z1 < z2 + 1
mean(hits)
#> [1] 0.76129
binom.test(sum(hits), length(hits), conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
#> [1] 0.7578002 0.7647549
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.99

Part (b) is an indicator, so binom.test. For the exact check: \(Z_1 - Z_2\) is Normal with mean 0 and variance \(1 + 1 = 2\), so \[P(Z_1 - Z_2 < 1) = \Phi(1/\sqrt{2})\]

pnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(2))
#> [1] 0.7602499

Two calls to rnorm, and the “double integral” never looked like one. The same recipe runs in any dimension — and the video showed its error rate does not depend on the dimension.

6. When the recipe breaks

The video stated conditions: \(\text{E}\left(h(X)\right) < \infty\) and \(\text{E}\left(h(X)^2\right) < \infty\). This exercise is about what happens when the second one fails.

Exercise

Estimate \[\theta = \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{1 + x^2} \, dx\] using Exp(1) draws, so \(h(x) = e^{x} / (1 + x^2)\). The true value is \(\pi/2 \approx 1.5708\).

  1. Run the estimator with \(n = 100{,}000\) five separate times (replicate helps). Do the answers agree with each other? With the truth?
  2. The estimator is unbiased — we proved that in the video. So what is going wrong? Look at \(\text{E}\left(h(X)^2\right)\).
  3. Would increasing \(n\) fix this?

Solution

h <- function(x) { exp(x) / (1 + x^2) }
replicate(5, mean(h(rexp(100000))))
#> [1] 1.512857 1.515777 1.586831 1.550898 1.562523
pi / 2
#> [1] 1.570796

The five runs disagree wildly, and typically all sit below the truth, with occasional runs far above it.

The variance condition fails: \[\text{E}\left(h(X)^2\right) = \int_0^\infty \frac{e^{2x}}{(1+x^2)^2} \, e^{-x} \, dx = \int_0^\infty \frac{e^{x}}{(1+x^2)^2} \, dx = \infty\] since \(e^x\) beats any polynomial. Rare draws far in the tail carry astronomically large \(h\) values: most runs miss them (estimate too low) and an occasional run catches one (estimate far too high). With infinite variance the CLT does not apply, so the confidence interval machinery is invalid — the intervals are narrow and wrong.

Increasing \(n\) does not fix it. The problem is the mismatch between where \(1/(1+x^2)\) has its mass (heavy tail) and where Exp(1) samples (light tail). The fix is a better sampling distribution — that is the subject of the next video (importance sampling).
